A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ST-WebAgentBench. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across substantial reformatting and renumbering.

before.justification: v3 reports original evaluations of AWM, WorkArena Legacy, and WebVoyager, including completion metrics, policy violations, and observed failure cases in Section 4 and the appendices.

after.justification: v4 retains those evaluations and additionally reports dimension ablations, policy-load analyses, and expert-panel and incident-coverage findings.

M1.justification: The benchmark retains the same six safety dimensions, policy-template families, evaluation components, BrowserGym integration, and simulated human confirmation. Expanded construction explanations and reformatted implementation examples do not establish a changed procedure. The future policy-aware architecture is also retained.

E1.justification: Agent evaluation retains GitLab, ShoppingAdmin, SuiteCRM, and the same safety scenario families. Table 2 retains 47, 8, and 167 tasks respectively. Policy-load analyses regroup existing tasks, while Appendix B elaborates the enterprise input behind dimension selection; neither establishes a new agent-evaluation domain or task family.

E2.justification: Both versions evaluate AWM, WorkArena Legacy, and WebVoyager. The historical WebArena leaderboard is retained, and newly cited agents and safety benchmarks do not participate as additional evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: v4 introduces dimension-deletion recomputation and four policy-load bins: 1, 2–3, 4–5, and more than 5. Table 2 substantially revises policy counts and changes average policies from 5.4 to 4.0 for GitLab and 2.0 to 3.0 for ShoppingAdmin. Section 3.3 changes Risk Ratio normalization from policy source to dimension. Table 1 changes 234 tasks to 222, matching the retained application totals; these reported revisions do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 provides illustrative failures and anticipates difficulties with increasing policy loads. v4 retains those cases and adds a quantitative leave-one-dimension-out analysis testing each dimension's contribution (Table 3), plus policy-load sensitivity analysis testing compliance scalability (Appendix C and Figure 3).

E5.justification: v4 first explicitly states that the benchmark was executed once per agent; it does not establish increased repetitions. The new scalability analysis reports p < 0.001 and a slope of 0.11 ± 0.02. Figure 3 mentions omitted ±1 standard-error bars, but calculation details and uncertainty intervals for the main agent comparisons remain absent.

E6.justification: Figure 2 retains the main performance bars and rankings. New results include dimension-ablation correlation increases of 0.02–0.15, CuP declining from 18.2% to 7.1% across policy-load groups, and expert-mention and incident-coverage statistics, including 95% joint coverage. Separately, v4 changes AWM's consent risk in prose from 44% to 0.44% while retaining 37 breaches; this is a reporting discrepancy, not demonstrated improved performance.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 replaces v3's constrained reward-maximization expression with an explicit admissible-action set requiring satisfaction of all three policy sources. Section 3.3 replaces the source-indexed Risk Ratio definition with dimension-specific normalization. The CuP and partial-completion concepts remain equivalent, and neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The central contributions—a public safety benchmark, policy-aware metrics, and evidence that current agents fall short of enterprise requirements—remain. v4 extends the stated empirical contributions to dimension importance and measured policy-load scalability, and newly characterizes the six dimensions as orthogonal.

C2.justification: v3 interprets low boundary risk as reduced propensity for unauthorized access; v4 instead hypothesizes that agents seldom reach the relevant workflow states, also using this explanation for WebVoyager's narrow completion–CuP gap. It adds architecture-related conjectures and explains policy-count imbalance. The conclusion expands generic scope limitations into English-only enterprise coverage, a single policy hierarchy, restricted adversarial coverage, and an explicit warning that the benchmark is not a deployment gatekeeper.

D1.justification: v4 specifies Apple M1 Pro hardware and 32 GB RAM and states that evaluated agents were used without code changes. Appendix B adds stakeholder roles, elicitation questions, coding procedures, consent, and data-handling information beyond v3's general account of enterprise collaboration. The project link, repository structure, and implementation examples largely already existed.

R1.justification: v4 substantially expands positioning against SafeAgentBench, Agent-SafetyBench, ASB, browser-agent jailbreak studies, and GUI-agent trustworthiness research. It explicitly contrasts their evaluation scopes with tracing policy violations to web UI actions. Additional responsible-AI, NIST, hallucination, and tool-error literature now grounds the six dimensions.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, policy hierarchy, dimension descriptions, metric explanations, and discussion/conclusion are extensively rewritten. Metrics receive separate formula-led descriptions, appendices are reorganized into A–G, the ethics statement moves after the references, and a NeurIPS checklist is added.

P2.justification: The document adopts substantially different conference formatting and reflows its displays. Figures 1 and 2 are redrawn, Table 2 merges security and robustness columns, and new ablation, expert-summary, and scalability displays appear. Appendix code figures become numbered code tables, configuration listings are extensively restyled, and retained screenshots are relocated.

improvement.justification: v4 improves research context, construction documentation, and specific limitations, while adding potentially useful ablation and scalability evidence. However, the new analyses leave aggregation and uncertainty procedures unresolved: Figure 3 plots completion rates around 32–35% without explaining their relationship to the reported 24.3% aggregate, and its omitted-error-bar caption conflicts with the checklist's reporting claim. The 44% to 0.44% consent-risk change adds another inconsistency. These benefits and reporting problems prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
